# tekne-wf

`wf` (`@tekne/wf`): the studio's flow for parallel coding agents. An orchestrator, a Claude Code session in a project's main checkout, starts agents in herdr worktrees where the person sees them, watches them, checks and ships their work. Every project gets the same flow; its own preparation and gates live in its `wf.config.ts`.

This file holds for every agent; `CLAUDE.md` is a link to it.

## Shared rules

The project section below wins where the two differ.

### Knowledge: one fact, one place

| Information | Home |
|---|---|
| how it is now | the topic doc |
| why, and what was rejected | a decision |
| what comes next, in order; a problem with a known fix, however small | the roadmap |
| what waits on someone's answer; a problem without a chosen fix | an open question |
| how agents work | AGENTS.md, or the config its blocks render; docs link to it, never restate it |
| what changed, line by line | git |

An agent's own memory is none of these homes: the next agent never reads it. A decision touches at most three places: the topic doc, the decision, and the roadmap or a question. Each says only its own fact and links to the others, all in the commit of the change.

### kb: decisions, questions and docs

Decisions and open questions are one file each, written by `kb` (`bun kb --help`). Every list (indexes, the docs map, the sidebar) is built when read: never edit one by hand.

- **Before changing something,** ask why it is so: `kb why <doc.md#section | path>` or `kb search <terms>`.
- **Decision:** only for a choice with a plausible alternative someone would propose again, which Rejected names; without one, the why goes in a code comment or the topic doc. One choice each, the title stating it, three to six lines: `kb decision new "<title>" --decision "<what>" --why "<why>" --rejected "<the alternatives and why not>" --lives-in <doc.md#section>`.
- **Change of mind:** a new decision with `--supersedes <old id>` (`--amends` when the old one stays partly true); never rewrite the old one to say something else.
- **Open question,** the day it comes up: `kb question add "<question>" --group <group> --owner <who> --unblocks "<what waits on it>" --context <doc.md#section>`.
- **Checked with whoever unblocks it:** `kb question review <id>` (or `--group <group>`).
- **Answered:** `kb decision new ... --resolves <question id>`; the new state goes into the topic doc.
- **`kb check`** before committing docs; `kb gen` rewrites the generated blocks.

### Sessions: every turn rereads the whole conversation

- At the end of a task, or once the session has grown long, write what the next session needs in its home (the table above), then start fresh, or ask the person to.
- Read only what you need: `kb why` or `kb search` before a whole doc, a line range before a whole file, a narrowed search before a dump.
- A wide search goes to a subagent when the harness has one: it returns the conclusion, not the files.

### Writing docs and comments

- Say what the thing is and what to do. A prohibition comes with the way: "never X; use Y".
- Present only: the system as it is today; the past lives in git (what) and in decisions (why). No "used to", "removed", "no longer".
- Changed or removed code: in the same commit, rewrite or delete every comment and doc about it.
- Comments say why; the code says what.
- Concise: direct sentences, tables and lists when they fit. One file, one topic.

### Evidence before claims

- "Done", "fixed" and "passing" come after running the command in this turn and reading its output. Report the command and what it printed, and a skipped step as skipped.
- A visible change is looked at (screenshot or browser) before it is called done: tests prove only what they cover.
- Bug: reproduce it, find the cause, then fix. A bug from real use that earns a test gets one that fails before the fix and passes after. After three fixes that did not hold, question the approach instead of writing a fourth.
- Review feedback: check each point against the code before applying it, and answer a wrong one with evidence. Agreement is not a reply.

### Working with the person

- A feature that replaces a process the client already runs (spreadsheet, script, someone's routine): first a portrait of how it works today, validated with them; then a proposal in a separate document; the spec and the docs come after.
- A question gets an answer, the size of the question. Change something only when asked; when the answer shows a fix the person would obviously want, offer it in one line.
- Look around what you touch: stale, duplicated, inconsistent or more complex than needed. Small and same topic: fix it in the same commit and say so; bigger: point it out and propose.
- Ask one question at a time, with your recommendation, when the choice is genuinely theirs; otherwise pick the conventional option, say so, and go on.
- Destructive or outward-facing actions (deleting data, pushing to a shared environment, sending messages) wait for an explicit yes.

### Commits

- Conventional Commits (`feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `chore`, `refactor`); the type drives the release: `feat` minor, `fix` patch, `BREAKING CHANGE` major. The project section names the language of the description.
- `wip` never reaches the integration branch: retype or squash before merging.
- Commits and pull requests end at their content: no `Co-Authored-By` trailer, no "Generated with" footer.

### Roadmap

- **What comes next:** `kb roadmap`, in order. A task goes to `docs/roadmap.md`: a wish is one line under `## Later`; what comes next is a `###` item under `## Now`, in its place in the order, with its `**Done when:**` line.
- What waits on someone is an open question with `--unblocks roadmap.md#<item>`; the page keeps no blocked section.
- An item leaves the page in the commit that meets its `**Done when:**` line, and what it built lives in the topic doc; dropping one is a decision that says why. The method: `kb guide roadmap`.

### Parallel agents: wf

One orchestrator, a Claude Code session in the main checkout on `main`, leads the agents. Each task, whoever brings it, gets its own worktree, branch and agent, in a herdr pane the person watches, and a follow-up on a task goes to its agent; never two agents in one working directory. Never merge, push or close a worktree from inside it: the orchestrator ships it. `bun wf` runs the flow; when `ask`, `tell` or `report` prints a SendMessage, send it. For the rest of herdr (layout, reading a screen, focus), use `herdr` (`herdr --skill`).

Before anything with wf (a spawn, a question, a report, a ship, a doubt about the flow), run `bun wf --skill`: it prints the rules for the checkout it runs in, the agent's in a worktree and the orchestrator's in the main checkout; `--all` prints both.

## This project

### Where things are

| Read | For |
|---|---|
| `docs/portrait.md` | how the flow ran before `wf`, and what it taught |
| `docs/proposal.md` | what `wf` is, how the flow runs and what stays out |
| `docs/decisions/` | why each choice, over the alternatives it turned down (`bun kb search`, `bun kb why`) |
| `docs/spec.md` | each command, the config, the state, the tests |
| `docs/watch.md`, `docs/ship.md` | how `wf watch` wakes the orchestrator; how `wf ship` tests and delivers |
| `docs/herdr.md` | what `wf` calls and reads of herdr, and the plugin |
| `docs/release.md` | how a version is cut and published |
| `docs/roadmap.md` | what `wf` changes next, shipped as one release at the end of a round |
| `templates/rules.md` | the rules `wf gen` writes into each project's `AGENTS.md` |
| `templates/header.md` | the header `wf spawn` sends with each task |

### Commands

| For | Command |
|---|---|
| run the CLI from this checkout | `bun wf <command>` |
| type-check | `bun run check` |
| unit and ship tests | `bun run test` |
| the contract with the installed herdr (opens and closes one workspace) | `bun run test:herdr` |
| release: version, CHANGELOG, tag; CI publishes to `npm.tekne.studio` (needs the `NPM_TOKEN` secret) | `bun run release`, in the main checkout, on `main` and clean |

### Rules of this code

- **herdr lives behind `src/herdr.ts`.** It is the only file in `src/` that runs `herdr`; it reads herdr's JSON and echoes each command. A herdr change is fixed there and in the contract test (`contract/`). The plugin (`herdr/plugin.ts`) reads what herdr hands it and asks herdr only for a pane's folder; the rest goes through `wf`.
- **The flow's verbs are `wf`'s own.** Rules and configs name `wf` commands, never herdr commands for the flow; outside the flow, agents use herdr directly.
- **Never answer for the person**: no command answers an approval or a trust dialog, and nothing writes `~/.claude.json`.
- **Never push or publish from a command**: `ship` stops at the fast-forward; pushing waits for the person.
- **Tests run without the person's herdr**: `tests/` uses the fake in `tests/fake-herdr.ts` through `HERDR_BIN_PATH`. Only `contract/` talks to the real one.
- Bun runs the TypeScript directly; no build step, no runtime dependencies.

### Writing and commits

- Docs, comments, CLI messages and commit descriptions in English.
- This repository and the `@tekne/wf` package are public: docs, decisions, comments, tests and commits name no other project of the studio and none of its details (names, paths, people, data). Describe the case by its shape instead: "a project whose E2E and browser suites take 4 minutes".
- Commit types are kb's with `test`, lower case, in the present tense; while below 1.0, a breaking change is minor.
